events.title: The death of St. Ferdinand III of Castile
events.shortBlurb: The king who had taken Córdoba and Seville from the Moors and turned their great mosques into cathedrals died in his city of Seville…
body: On 30 May 1252 St. Ferdinand III, king of Castile and León, died at Seville, the city he had won for Christendom four years before; the Franciscans keep his feast on this day. He was buried in Seville's great cathedral before the image of the Blessed Virgin, clothed at his own request in the habit of the Third Order of St. Francis, and his body is said to remain incorrupt.

Born near Salamanca, the son of Alfonso IX of León and of Berengaria of Castile — and so the first cousin of St. Louis IX of France — he became king of Castile in 1217 by his mother's renunciation and of León in 1230, joining the two crowns for good. The highest aims of his life, says the old account, were the propagation of the faith and the liberation of Spain: he took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248, the greatest joys of his life, and made their great mosques cathedrals of Our Lady; at his death only Granada and Alicante remained in Moorish hands.

In the conquered towns he founded bishoprics and re-established Catholic worship, built churches, monasteries, and hospitals, and gave Spain the University of Salamanca. In camp he lived, it was said, like a religious in the cloister — fasting strictly, wearing a rough hairshirt, and spending the nights before battle in prayer. Clement X canonized him in 1671.
